title: Introducing VMware solution on Google Cloud
raw_text: Many organizations with workloads on VMware are looking for ways to expedite their data center exits, migrate and modernize their mission-critical workloads, or simply leverage the cloud as a secondary disaster recovery site. But they want to do so without altering existing operational playbooks. Today, we are announcing the general availability of the VMware solution on Google Cloud, part of the Google Cloud Modernize portfolio, giving you full administrative authority for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated Google Cloud bare metal. This new deployment model complements our existing Google-managed service, offering you greater flexibility and architectural choice for running VMware workloads in Google Cloud. With this new self managed offering, organizations with dedicated operational practices maintain direct control over their virtualization stack, specific maintenance windows, and custom integration with third-party monitoring and management tools. The launch of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x by Broadcom is a key driver behind this self-managed deployment option. Featuring a unified VCF control plane for end-to-end stack deployment and lifecycle management, this solution enables Google Cloud customers to directly leverage Broadcom's latest innovations and fully maximize their licensing investments in VMware Cloud Foundation. “Customers want the agility of Google Cloud without rearchitecting their VMware environments or abandoning the operational practices they have invested in. With the new VMware solution on Google Cloud, VCF license portability allows customers to bring their existing subscriptions and run their VMware workloads unchanged, with complete administrative control on dedicated Z3 bare metal and the ability to apply Google Cloud commitments and discounts to optimize their costs.” - Abhay Kumar, Global Head of Hyperscalers, VMware Cloud Foundation Division, Broadcom Expanding deployment choices for VMware workloads When it comes to VMware workloads, Google Cloud now offers two distinct choices tailored to your priorities, letting you choose the operational model that matches your workloads’ characteristics and the levels of control you need: Google Cloud VMware Engine, and the VMware solution on Google Cloud. Capability Google Cloud VMware Engine VMware solution on Google Cloud Target workloads Turnkey operations prioritizing operational simplicity and offloaded maintenance Architectural flexibility for teams requiring full stack customization and direct ownership Underlying software VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2 VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x Administrative access Role-based vCenter administrative privileges Full root administrative access across ESXi, vCenter, NSX Manager, and rest of the VCF components Lifecycle management Automated patching, updates, and monitoring managed by Google Customer-or partner-driven updates via VCF Operations Management tools Licensing model Bring Your Own License (BYOL) portable VCF subscriptions Bring Your Own License (BYOL) portable VCF subscriptions Hardware platform VMware Engine ve1 and ve2 node families Dedicated Compute Engine (GCE) bare metal instances (e.g Z3) High-performance architecture on bare metal The self-managed VMware solution is deployed on dedicated GCE Z3 bare metal instances (z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal). Powered by 2.2 GHz - 4th Generation Intel Xeon Processors (Sapphire Rapids) processors, each node delivers: 96 physical cores (192 hyper-threads) 1.5 TB RAM 72 TB all-flash NVMe storage 200 Gbps networking Operating natively within Google Cloud alongside GCE and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), this architecture provides high bandwidth and low-latency networking for transactional databases and direct access to native Google Cloud services, including BigQuery, the Gemini platform, Cloud Run, and more. The solution's storage architecture is built on VMware vSAN hyperconverged infrastructure using high-performance, all-flash NVMe storage from Z3 nodes. Beyond standard storage, these drives can also be utilized for NVMe memory tiering. In addition to vSAN, the solution also supports NetApp volumes. "VMware solution on Google Cloud gives enterprises greater control, choice, and architectural freedom as they move to the cloud. We are excited to expand our partnership with Google Cloud by offering NetApp Volumes as an external datastore. Together, we’re helping customers confidently migrate their VMware workloads and data to Google Cloud while retaining the flexibility, performance and data management capabilities they rely on .” - Pravjit Tiwana, SVP/GM, Cloud Storage, NetApp Realizing clear customer value and TCO optimization Pairing VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 with Google Cloud’s Z3 bare metal infrastructure delivers significant economic and operational efficiency : Commercial flexibility and BYOL: Bring portable Broadcom VCF subscriptions while allocating Google Cloud commitments and Flexible Committed Use Discounts (Flex CUDs) toward Z3 bare metal shapes. NVMe memory tiering: Tiering between DDR memory (Tier 0) and high-speed local NVMe (Tier 1) can reduce server TCO by up to 40%. vSAN Express Storage Architecture (ESA): Utilizing high-throughput local NVMe storage reduces storage TCO by up to 39% compared to traditional external arrays. Active live patching: Up to 80% live patching coverage for critical security updates reduces planned maintenance downtime. Architectural and commercial differentiation In addition to the above-mentioned benefits, Google Cloud provides distinct operational and technical advantages that go beyond standard cloud hosting: Triple-governance operational choices: Select from Google-, customer-, or partner- frameworks to align precisely with your operating model. Granular capacity sizing: Access bare metal shapes across GCE hardware families to optimize utilization resulting in a lower TCO. Global virtual networking: Peer complex multi-edge and multi-VPC topologies natively via Andromeda and Network Connectivity Center (NCC). AI Acceleration: Seamlessly connect systems of record directly to BigQuery and Gemini platform to enable AI capabilities. What our customers are saying “Our early assessment shows significant potential. Separating the hardware lifecycle from the virtualization layer gives us the ability to scale bare-metal capacity in minutes, while still retaining full administrative control. This provides the flexibility of the cloud with the level of control we require from our infrastructure platforms.” - Scott Ronan, Senior Director of Platforms, Databases & Cloud, GXO Logistics Partner-managed ecosystem For organizations that prefer managed services, Google Cloud partners with organizations with expertise across both Google Cloud and VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) to provide end-to-end support for self-managed VMware solution including: Day 0: Architecture planning and solution design Day 1: Deployment and migration execution Day 2 and beyond: Ongoing lifecycle management and operations Delivered via professional or managed services contracts, you can collaborate with your preferred providers or tap into our featured partner offerings on the self-managed VMware solution: Accenture , Advanced Business Computing , Cognizant , Devoteam , HCL , IBM , Infosys , Insight , LiverX , ModernZ , Pellera , Quantiphi , Tata Consultancy Services , Wipro , and Xtravirt . Getting started VMware solution on Google Cloud is generally available across 22 Google Cloud regions, with planned expansion to more regions in upcoming quarters. To get started: Visit the VMware solution on Google Cloud webpage for more details. Review the solution overview and core concepts on the documentation page. Reach out to your Google Cloud account team or an authorized partner to evaluate this offering.

title: Powering the agentic enterprise with latest innovations in Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud
raw_text: For decades, core enterprise operations — from global supply chains and financial ledgers to billing engines — have relied on the performance and transactional integrity of Oracle databases. Today at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Google Cloud and Oracle are expanding our partnership across the AI stack — spanning AI compute and infrastructure (including making Google TPUs available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure), enterprise data, and agentic AI — by deepening the integration between Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud, Google’s Agentic Data Cloud , and Gemini Enterprise. By unifying Oracle’s mission-critical operational data and applications with Google Cloud’s data and AI ecosystem — including BigQuery, Gemini Enterprise, and Gemini models — enterprises can move beyond static analytics and build autonomous, agentic workflows. This architecture breaks down traditional data silos, giving agents direct, secure, and real-time access to the foundational enterprise data required to drive real-world action. Foundational building blocks for agentic AI To unlock production-grade agentic AI, enterprises need more than raw model capability — they need strong database connectivity, unified data governance, and rich semantic context working together as a cohesive foundation. First announced at Google Cloud Next '26, the following core capabilities serve as the building blocks for building conversational intelligence, end-to-end governance, and autonomous agent environments on Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud: Remote MCP Server with Data API : The Remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server for Oracle workloads — powered by the IAM-governed ExecuteSQL Data API — is now generally available. Together, they provide a unified, standardized interface that enables AI agents, Google Cloud services, and enterprise applications to securely run SQL and interact directly with Oracle databases. By resolving database credentials automatically through Secret Manager and enforcing Google Cloud IAM policies, this capability eliminates the need for custom natural-language-to-SQL middleware, bastion VMs, or plaintext passwords. Knowledge Catalog integration : Google Cloud’s Knowledge Catalog integration, currently in preview, unifies enterprise metadata discovery and governance across Oracle databases and the broader Google Agentic Data Cloud. By automatically cataloging schemas and business metadata, organizations can enforce consistent access controls, track data provenance, and supply the rich semantic context that agents require to reason accurately over complex operational data. Click here to sign-up for this feature. Gemini connector for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud Building directly on the foundational capabilities discussed above, we’re also announcing the preview of Gemini connector for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud . With this native integration, business users and developers can interact directly with their Oracle databases on Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud using natural language queries right inside the Gemini app. Behind the scenes, Gemini automatically leverages Knowledge Catalog to discover, search, and ground responses strictly in the governed Oracle data each user is authorized to access — turning complex operational databases into an intuitive, conversational experience without compromising enterprise security. Click here to sign-up for this feature. Oracle in Gemini and Gemini in Oracle Beyond direct database queries, Google Cloud and Oracle are connecting agentic workflows across the broader application layer — bringing Oracle data into Gemini Enterprise and embedding Gemini models natively inside Oracle applications: Oracle in Gemini Enterprise: Available today, Oracle in Gemini Enterprise introduces conversational analytics, cross-cloud database connectors, and domain-aware agents — including the new Oracle AI Database Agent in Gemini Enterprise. Anchored by over 135 pre-built operational and developer skills and standardized MCP connectivity with zero plaintext credentials, enterprises can orchestrate multi-agent workflows across JD Edwards, E-Business Suite, NetSuite, and Oracle Fusion without custom SQL or brittle middleware. Gemini models in Oracle applications : Concurrently, Gemini frontier reasoning is embedded directly into Oracle Fusion AI Agent Studio , Fusion Claw , Oracle Fusion Applications, and NetSuite — combining Oracle database intelligence with Gemini’s agentic capabilities to automate execution across transactional systems of record. Partner-ready agentic blueprints: To help organizations rapidly deploy these governed workflows, Google Cloud and Oracle are collaborating with leading partners and global systems integrators — including Argano , Automus , Calfus , HCL , IBM , Infosys , LTM , Pythian , TCS , and Tessell — who provide pre-built operational skills, custom MCP connectors, and industry blueprints for production-grade agentic architectures. Empowering choice with lakehouse, streaming, and federation Every enterprise has distinct architectural priorities, latency thresholds, and governance requirements when connecting operational Oracle data to BigQuery and AI workloads. Rather than prescribing a one-size-fits-all integration pattern, Google Cloud and Oracle offer a complete spectrum of data unification choices so customers can select — or combine — the exact approach that best fits their workload and use case: Bi-directional Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse and Oracle AI Lakehouse Modern enterprise data architectures are increasingly multi-cloud and grounded in open standards. Building on our strategic partnership, Google Cloud and Oracle delivered a key innovation earlier this year to support cross-cloud data interoperability powered by open Apache Iceberg standard: integrating Google’s borderless Lakehouse with Oracle AI Lakehouse . This work enabled the borderless Lakehouse to read Apache Iceberg tables created by Oracle AI Lakehouse across any public cloud or on-premises environment, leveraging catalogs and storage supported by both platforms. Today, we are advancing it further by making it fully bi-directional with Oracle Access to Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse (preview) . Now, Oracle Autonomous AI Database and Google’s borderless Lakehouse (powered by BigQuery and Managed Spark) can directly query and execute write/DML operations on shared Apache Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage, completely eliminating the need for ETL or data replication. By utilizing a Lakehouse runtime REST catalog integrated into Oracle via DBMS_CATALOG , this bi-directional integration delivers an open-standards storage framework while empowering analytical teams (using BigQuery and Gemini) and operational teams (using Oracle SQL) to collaborate over a single, unified source of truth. You can click here to sign-up for this feature. Sub-second CDC streaming with OCI GoldenGate For organizations that prefer to continuously reflect mission-critical operational data inside BigQuery for high-scale analytics and AI, real-time change data capture (CDC) provides an immediate competitive edge. Through native OCI GoldenGate integration , CDC events are extracted directly from Oracle redo logs without touching table blocks or adding overhead to transactional workloads. Transactions stream securely across Google Cloud private networks straight into BigQuery managed tables, delivering sub-second analytical freshness to power Gemini, feature stores, and live business intelligence dashboards, while also streamlining migrations from on-premises environments to Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud. BigQuery query federation with Oracle When workloads call for on-demand operational visibility or infrequent cross-estate joins without moving data, BigQuery query federation with Oracle, in preview, enables real-time, in-place analytics directly against live Oracle databases. title: Securely connecting Gemini Enterprise to Snowflake data
raw_text:
Enterprise AI needs to go beyond simple chat interfaces. To provide real value, AI agents must access your data warehouses to generate actionable insights, all while maintaining strict security and data governance. This guide explores how to build a secure bridge between Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise and Snowflake. By using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), you can empower your agent to act as an assistant that understands natural language, generates precise SQL via Snowflake Cortex and executes queries with user-level permissions. Choosing the right integration pattern Direct Connection vs. custom orchestration The Google ADK architecture demonstrated in this post represents the advanced / custom orchestration pattern. It is designed for developers building complex, multi-agent systems on Google Cloud, such as workflows that combine Snowflake insights with external enterprise tools, custom reasoning loops, or cross-platform state management in Gemini Agent Engine. For standard enterprise basic use cases where you want to connect Gemini Enterprise directly to Snowflake use the joint solutions mentioned in this link . The architectural approach This architecture allows a business user to ask questions like, "What were our top 5 selling items in Texas last quarter?" Rather than exposing raw SQL execution to the client, the agent delegates both query generation and execution to a governed Snowflake Cortex Agent exposed through the Snowflake MCP server: Governed translation : The ADK agent passes the user's natural language question to the Snowflake MCP server, which invokes the Cortex Agent (CORTEX_AGENT_RUN) backed by Cortex Analyst semantic view. Direct execution within the governed boundary : The Cortex Agent translates the question into SQL and executes it directly inside Snowflake using the authenticated user's OAuth session and role privileges, returning the structured results to the ADK agent. This approach provides deterministic text-to-SQL translation mapped to your corporate semantic definitions, keeps query execution inside Snowflake's governed boundary, and reduces the risk of schema hallucinations or unvalidated SQL execution. System architecture flow The diagram below illustrates the trust boundaries and the numbered flow of execution between the Gemini Enterprise app and Snowflake ecosystems. Detailed execution sequence To highlight how the agent delegates natural language query translation and governed execution to the Snowflake Cortex Agent over MCP, see the sequence diagram below: Step 1: Setting up the Snowflake security integration A major risk in enterprise AI is granting the model broad access via a generic service account, which could allow users to bypass security restrictions. We solve this by using OAuth 2.0 to perform user impersonation. First, establish a confidential OAuth client in Snowflake to protect the client secret. The snippet below configures the security integration inside Snowflake: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN; 
CREATE OR REPLACE SECURITY INTEGRATION <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME> 
TYPE = OAUTH 
ENABLED = TRUE 
OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM 
OAUTH_CLIENT_TYPE = 'CONFIDENTIAL' 
-- Google Cloud's official handshake receiver address: 
OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI = 'https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/oauth-redirect' 
OAUTH_ISSUE_REFRESH_TOKENS = TRUE 
-- Let the connection stay alive for 90 days (max Snowflake allowed limit) 
OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY = 7776000;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc590344b90>)])]> To retrieve the generated client credentials needed for the Google Cloud configuration, run the following command in Snowflake: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Retrieve OAuth Client ID and Client Secret
SELECT SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS('<SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>');"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc57294ced0>)])]> Step 2: Data governance and access control Apply the principle of least privilege by creating a dedicated role for your agent inside Snowflake. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
-- 1. Create a dedicated role
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
GRANT ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME> TO USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME>; 
USE ROLE SYSADMIN;
-- 2. Grant structural access
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE <DATABASE_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 3. Grant compute access
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE <WAREHOUSE_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 4 .Grant access to the semantic layer
GRANT SELECT, REFERENCES ON SEMANTIC VIEW <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SEMANTIC_VIEW_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 5. Grant select privileges on underlying raw data tables
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572377410>)])]> IMPORTANT The user context must have SELECT privileges on the physical tables backing the semantic view. Granting access only to the semantic view will cause runtime errors during query execution. If granting direct access to base tables is not permitted by your security policy, place a Snowflake Secure View over the physical tables and build the Semantic View on top of it. Because Snowflake views execute with Owner's Rights , the user's GenAI role only needs SELECT privileges on the Secure View and Semantic View rather than the raw tables. Snowflake OAuth tokens capture and bind to the user's DEFAULT_ROLE and DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE at the exact moment of authorization. If a user authorizes the connection before these defaults are configured, the session will be locked to the wrong role(role available at that time) and query execution will fail if the intended role will not have required privileges. Set defaults(as shown below) prior to authorizing in Gemini Enterprise. Authorize connection: Have the user perform the one-time OAuth authorization in Gemini Enterprise. (Optional) Revert defaults: Once authorized, the user can safely revert their default role and warehouse in Snowflake back to their standard operational preferences. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "ALTER USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME> SET DEFAULT_ROLE = '<GENAI_ROLE_NAME>';
ALTER USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME> SET DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = '<WAREHOUSE_NAME>';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572376450>)])]> Step 3: Provisioning the Cortex Agent and MCP server inside Snowflake Next, create a governed Cortex Agent in Snowflake using your semantic view, then provision an MCP server that exposes the agent via the CORTEX_AGENT_RUN tool type. This approach delegates both SQL generation and query execution to Snowflake while enforcing the caller's OAuth identity and role permissions. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'USE DATABASE <DATABASE_NAME>;
USE SCHEMA <SCHEMA_NAME>;
USE ROLE SYSADMIN;

-- 1. Create the Cortex Agent over your semantic view
CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT <AGENT_NAME>
 COMMENT = 'Governed data assistant for business queries'
 PROFILE = '{"cortex_analyst": {"semantic_models": ["<DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SEMANTIC_VIEW_NAME>"]}}';

-- 2. Provision the MCP Server exposing the Cortex Agent
CREATE OR REPLACE MCP SERVER <SERVER_NAME>
FROM SPECIFICATION $$
tools:
 - name: "run_cortex_agent"
 type: "CORTEX_AGENT_RUN"
 identifier: "<DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<AGENT_NAME>"
 title: "Cortex Agent Assistant"
 description: "Converts natural language questions into SQL and executes them directly within Snowflake using the caller's OAuth session permissions."
$$;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572375450>)])]> ISOLATION & GOVERNANCE NOTE: By using CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, query generation and execution remain fully contained within Snowflake's governed security boundary. Avoid exposing raw execution tools like SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL to external clients, as doing so introduces unnecessary security surface area and bypasses centralized Cortex Agent governance. Step 4: Locating and constructing the MCP server URL The ADK code requires the endpoint URL of your Snowflake-managed MCP server. Now that the server is provisioned, you must first grant access to the server, and then you can retrieve its exact endpoint URL using the following query in a Snowflake worksheet: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- 1. Grant access to the Cortex Agent and the MCP server
USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
GRANT USAGE ON AGENT <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<AGENT_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
GRANT USAGE ON MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 2. View the MCP URL
DESCRIBE MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME>;
-- Or:
DESC MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572377bd0>)])]> In the command output, inspect the metadata properties to locate the endpoint link. The URL is structured as follows: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'https://<org_name>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com/api/v2/databases/<database_name>/schemas/<schema_name>/mcp-servers/<server_name>'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572375290>)])]> Step 5: Connecting via Google ADK With the MCP Server created and its URL resolved, write your agent code using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK). In your Python code, define the unique identifier AUTH_ID (e.g. snowflake_oauth_conn) that the agent will use to extract user credentials. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import os
import re
from typing import Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_toolset import McpToolset
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import StreamableHTTPConnectionParams
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

# Define the Auth ID first in your code. 
# You will use this exact name when registering the agent in the Google Cloud Console.
# Gemini Enterprise maps the authorization token to this identifier in the ToolContext.
AUTH_ID = "snowflake_oauth_conn" 

# 1. OAuth Header Extraction:
# Define a callback to dynamically extract the user's OAuth token injected by Gemini Enterprise 
# and generate the Authorization headers required to authenticate with the Snowflake MCP.
def get_auth_headers(tool_context: Optional[ToolContext] = None) -> dict: 
 """ 
 OAuth Handling Callback: Dynamically extracts the user's OAuth token injected by Gemini Enterprise and generates the headers required to authenticate with the Snowflake MCP. 
 """ 
 token = None 
 if tool_context and hasattr(tool_context, "state"): 
 try: 
 # Parse the state dictionary injected by Gemini Enterprise containing authorization states 
 state_dict = tool_context.state.to_dict() if hasattr(tool_context.state, 'to_dict') else tool_context.state 
 pattern = re.compile(fr".*{re.escape(AUTH_ID)}.*", re.IGNORECASE) 
 # Find the active token matching our Auth ID (snowflake_oauth_conn)
 matching_keys = [k for k in state_dict.keys() if pattern.match(k)] 
 if matching_keys: 
 token = state_dict.get(matching_keys[0]) 
 except Exception as e: 
 print(f"Warning: Failed to read ToolContext OAuth state: {e}") 
 # Return authorization headers. If token is None, requests to MCP will fail.
 return { 
 "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", 
 "Content-Type": "application/json", 
 "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream", 
 } 

# 2. MCP Initialization:
# Define the Snowflake MCP URL retrieved from 'DESCRIBE MCP SERVER' directly in the code:
MCP_SERVER_URL = "<YOUR_MCP_SERVER_URL>" # Replace with the URL retrieved from 'DESCRIBE MCP SERVER' 

# Initialize the Snowflake MCP Toolset using this URL.
snowflake_mcp = McpToolset( 
 connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams( 
 url=MCP_SERVER_URL 
 ), 
 header_provider=get_auth_headers
) 

# 3. Build the Agent:
# Construct the LlmAgent using the Gemini 2.5 Flash model and attach the Snowflake MCP Toolset.
root_agent = LlmAgent( 
 model="gemini-2.5-flash", 
 name="enterprise_data_analyst", 
 instruction=( 
 "You are an enterprise data analyst. Use the `enterprise_data_agent` tool " 
 "on the Snowflake MCP server to answer business questions. Pass the user's " 
 "natural language question to the tool, which translates it into SQL and " 
 "executes it directly within Snowflake's governed boundary, then present " 
 "the results clearly to the user." 
 ), 
 tools=[snowflake_mcp]
)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572374490>)])]> NOTE: The Python snippet above represents a plain/vanilla version of the agent setup. Depending on your organization's specific requirements, you should add robustness on top of this template (e.g., custom error handling, structured schemas, custom prompts, configurations, and additional tool wrappers). Step 6: Project structure and deployment To deploy your ADK agent to Agent Runtime in Agent Platform, organize your files in the following directory layout: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'snowflake_agent/
├── agent.py # The agent definition and MCP connection code (from Step 5)
├── __init__.py # Package initializer exposing the agent
├── .env # Environment configurations (Google Cloud Project, etc.)
└── requirements.txt # List of project dependencies (google-adk, etc.)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc59043d4d0>)])]> File details __init__.py: Exposes the root_agent object to the deployment CLI: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Snowflake ADK Agent package
from .agent import root_agent'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc572374450>)])]> .env: Declares environment configuration: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT="<YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID>"
GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION="<LOCATION>"
GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI="TRUE"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc59043c850>)])]> requirements.txt: Specifies dependencies: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'google-adk[mcp]==2.3.0
google-genai==2.10.0
pydantic-settings==2.14.2
google-cloud-aiplatform[agent_engines]>=1.50.0'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc59043d150>)])]> 2. Deploying via the CLI Rather than running complex custom Python scripts or manual container builds, you can deploy using the official Google Agents CLI (agents-cli). The CLI packages your code, sets up the server, and handles the deployment pipeline: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Deploy the agent to the Google Cloud Agent Runtime
agents-cli deploy --deployment-target agent_runtime'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc59043eb10>)])]> The CLI automatically handles the deployment lifecycle. Once complete, it outputs the unique project resource path (e.g., projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/reasoningEngines/RESOURCE_ID) which you will use to register the agent in the next step. TIP: For more information and advanced configuration options for ADK agent deployment, refer to: ADK Agent Runtime Deployment Guide ADK Deployment Reference Documentation Step 7: Registering the custom agent in Gemini Enterprise Once the agent code is ready and deployed, register the agent in the Google Cloud Console. Here, you will link the agent configuration and map the OAuth parameters retrieved from your Snowflake Security Integration. Extracting the OAuth Endpoints from Snowflake Run this query in Snowflake to extract the precise Token and Authorization endpoints: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc59043cc90>)])]> In the results, locate the values for the following properties: OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_ENDPOINT : Your Snowflake Authorization URI. OAUTH_TOKEN_ENDPOINT : Your Snowflake Token URI. 2. Registration steps in Google Cloud console Go to the Gemini Enterprise page in the console. Select the application you want to register the agent with. In the left navigation, click Agents , then click + Add agent . Select Add for Custom agent via Agent Platform . The Authorizations setup displays. Set up the Snowflake OAuth connection: Click Add authorization . Authorization name : Enter the exact ID you defined in your ADK code (e.g., snowflake_oauth_conn). This ensures the credentials map correctly to the code's AUTH_ID. Client ID & Client secret : Input the credentials you retrieved from Snowflake using the SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS query. Token URI : Input the exact token endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION. Authorization URI : Take the authorization endpoint value extracted from DESCRIBE SECURITY INTEGRATION and append ?response_type=code at the end (along with your client ID and scope query parameters, for example): code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'https://<org_name>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fvertexaisearch.cloud.google.com%2Foauth-redirect&scope=session%3Arole-any&response_type=code'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc59043e150>)])]> IMPORTANT Ensure the Authorization URI ends with &response_type=code (or ?response_type=code if there are no other parameters). This parameter is required by Google Cloud to trigger the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow. Click Done , then click Next . 6. Configure the agent properties: 7. Click Create to complete registration. Understanding identifier alignment ADK Code AUTH_ID <==> Google Cloud Authorization Name : The AUTH_ID in your Python script must exactly match the Authorization Name/ID you input during console registration. Because we write code first, we reuse the code-defined identifier during registration. Snowflake Security Integration Name (e.g. <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>) : This is purely a Snowflake-side database object name. It does not need to match the Google Cloud Authorization Name or the AUTH_ID in your ADK Python code. Get started By uniting the Gemini model’s reasoning capabilities, ADK's orchestration, and Snowflake's governed data layer, you can safely bring AI to your data. This architecture provides an agentic assistant that respects your security perimeters while delivering business value.

title: Scale agents securely with IAM Helper Agent Skills and MCP Tools
raw_text: As organizations adopt autonomous agents to build applications, securing identities and access has become more challenging. Developers relying on agents to provision cloud resources, write Terraform, and deploy microservices at machine-speed only find their CI/CD pipelines blo cked even faster as security friction scales. To help you get ahead of agentic-era Identity and Access Management, today we’re introducing IAM Helper. This suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows. As an agent-native orchestration and interface layer for Google Cloud IAM, it augments Google Cloud’s core IAM engines — including Policy Intelligence and Privileged Access Manager (PAM) — making IAM skills callable directly by autonomous code assistants, deployment pipelines, and custom agents. Using this functionality reduces the administrative overhead of maintaining least-privilege security and agent governance, while maximizing utility, and accelerating deployment. IAM Helper Agent Skills: Fast, secure deployment with automated governance Manual troubleshooting of permission blockers creates friction for engineering and administrators, while shortcuts can lead to broad agent over-permissioning that puts least privilege at risk. IAM Helper empowers agents to handle access management dynamically. It shifts the burden of policy evaluation away from human administrators and LLMs, offloading complex orchestration directly to the Google Cloud backend, to maximize token efficiency and prevent costly operational bottlenecks. Rather than operating as isolated utilities, IAM Helper Agent Skills guide agents through the cloud access lifecycle. These end-to-end workflows, helper scripts, and guardrails packaged using the open Agent Skills standard can orchestrate multiple underlying functions and APIs to resolve complex IAM tasks. They work across common agents (Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist, ADK, Claude Code, and Cursor). Built-in guardrails and real-world impact Every IAM Helper agent skill separates read-only discovery from policy changes: Diagnostics and simulations run automatically, while any change to access policies pauses for human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation based on customizable risk tiers. To see the value of IAM Helper in practice, consider how it transforms two everyday scenarios: Scaled user-assisted remediation : Suppose a developer's coding agent hits a 403 error while deploying a new application. Rather than filing a support ticket and idling, the agent uses iam-helper-for-troubleshooting to identify the missing Pub/Sub permission in seconds, then uses iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management to request a one-hour JIT grant, eliminating hours of debugging friction. Autonomous pipeline self-healing : An infrastructure agent encounters a permission block during a routine deployment pipeline. Rather than failing the build, the pipeline uses IAM Helper Agent skills to generate a revised, least-privilege policy, verifies against 90 days of logs via iam-helper-for-policy-simulator that active services won't break, and routes the change to an admin for quick approval. IAM Helper Agent Skills are designed for maximum token and cost efficiency, allowing agents to execute multi-step administrative operations autonomously. Authoring compliant, least-privilege policies : As DevOps engineers translate access requirements into JSON, YAML, or Terraform HCL, iam-helper-for-policy-management generates and validates IAM v1 allow bindings and IAM v2 deny rules. It automatically catches and blocks risky configs before they are applied, including public access (allUsers) and broad basic roles (roles/owner, roles/editor). Unblocking 403 errors in seconds : When an on-call engineer or deployment agent hits a cryptic 403 PERMISSION_DENIED error, iam-helper-for-troubleshooting identifies the exact missing permission or blocking rule in seconds. It adapts to the user’s role: Developers can check if they can unblock themselves locally or generate a structured ticket for their administrator (Requester flow), while security administrators can trace inherited allow and v2 deny rules across organization, folder, and project hierarchies to resolve the issue (Resolver flow). Simulating blast radius before rolling out changes : Before a platform engineer updates a policy or applies IAM Recommender role reductions, they need confidence that active workloads won't break. iam-helper-for-policy-simulator walks the agent through a structured plan, simulate, analyze, and apply flow, testing proposed changes against 90 days of historical access logs to confirm existing traffic won't be disrupted before any update takes effect. Elevating access just-in-time instead of granting standing privileges : When responders or maintenance agents need temporary production access, iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management manages the lifecycle of on-demand credentials through Privileged Access Manager (PAM). It supports requester, administrator, and approver workflows so elevated access is audited, time-bound, and automatically revoked once the task is done. While IAM Helper Agent Skills supply the high-level workflow logic, they are all based on a common set of foundational MCP Tools. Powered by Google Cloud IAM MCP tools Google Cloud IAM Helper MCP tools provide the backend connection through atomic, read-only functions exposed via Google-managed MCP servers across core IAM endpoints (Policy Troubleshooter, Policy Analyzer, Policy Simulator, and IAM v1/v2 APIs). Rather than requiring teams to write custom API wrappers, MCP tools give agents a standard way to query the cloud backend and get exact answers without parsing verbose policy documents in the prompt, maximizing token efficiency. Agents can dynamically discover and invoke these tools to execute basic operations like checking permissions or listing roles when custom logic is required. Because operations like hierarchy traversal, group expansion, and policy evaluation happen on dedicated IAM endpoints (spanning IAM v1 allow roles, IAM v2 deny, Policy Troubleshooter, and Policy Analyzer), skills run quickly and accurately with minimal token usage. Teams can also use these atomic MCP tools directly when writing their own custom Agent Skills, making it straightforward to combine Google Cloud's IAM capabilities with internal ticketing systems, custom compliance checks, and existing deployment pipelines. Getting started Accelerate your agentic workflows, reduce operational overhead, and bring intelligent, scalable security to your deployment pipelines. Start building with IAM Helper Agent skills today by exploring our Google Cloud Agent Skills Catalog and dive deeper with the official IAM documentation .

title: Bringing Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
raw_text: As AI workloads scale across every industry, organizations need compute options that optimize throughput, latency, and unit economics across the AI lifecycle. To meet this demand, Oracle and Google Cloud are partnering to bring Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), making OCI the first hyperscaler outside Google to offer TPUs. Together, we will deploy TPU capacity on OCI starting in the calendar year 2027. TPUs: Co-designed from silicon to software Google built its first TPU more than ten years ago on a clear product thesis: co-designing custom silicon alongside optical networking, power delivery, liquid cooling, and compiler software yields gains in performance per watt and total cost of ownership that isolated components cannot match. When customers have more choices of purpose-built compute across more clouds, the entire industry builds faster and operates more efficiently. We can’t wait to see what you build.

title: Google Cloud and NASA: Testing robotic systems for deep space missions
raw_text: As NASA advances its Artemis program to send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon, build a sustained human presence there with a Moon Base, and build on their foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars, crew safety and Earth-independent autonomy are paramount. An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges—including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes, making real-time medical guidance for crew nearly impossible. Last year, Google Public Sector shared progress on the development of the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant (CMO-DA) - an automated Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) designed to assist astronauts with real-time medical guidance in remote and isolated environments. Today, we are building on this innovation with the development of a proof-of-concept physical, robotic system that aims to support deep space missions and could assist astronauts during NASA missions. Optimizing crew time and safety The future Moon Base in the lunar South Pole region of the Moon is planned to support sustained human presence. Because every minute in space is a strictly limited resource, reducing the physical burden on astronauts to maximize their time for science and discovery is a top priority. To potentially address this challenge, NASA’s Human Research Program , Johnson Space Center Robotics Team, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) collaborated with Google Public Sector to develop a robotic system. By handling routine logistics, this system could free up astronauts to focus on what humans do best: complex science and discovery. To maximize its utility for a lean crew, the robotic system is designed as a versatile "payload" handler capable of managing cargo, logistics, and equipment. When not needed for routine maintenance like organizing tools or securing compartments, it can pivot to medical support. For example, if an astronaut experiences severe back pain—a potential symptom of kidney stones—the robot could retrieve and prepare an ultrasound machine. This enables the human crew medical officer to focus entirely on analyzing the scan and treating the patient. Adapting spatial awareness and vision-language-action models for robotic systems Operating safely alongside humans in confined spacecraft is a complex challenge. Unlike factory robots in fixed, human-free environments, space systems utilizing Super Intelligence (SI) require flexible, human-directed tools to safely adapt to close quarters. Because they must also rely on limited sensory input like cameras, JPL is adapting satellite situational awareness intelligence tools—originally designed to track objects in orbit—to help the robotic system navigate and understand its 3D surroundings. To test this safely at Johnson Space Center’s iMETRO facility, Google DeepMind’s MuJoCo simulator was used, which is an advanced physics engine that allows the SI to practice complex movements in a highly accurate virtual environment before touching real hardware. In a recent proof-of-concept technology demonstration, the robotic system was tasked with a complex "pick-and-place" maneuver to locate and move a medical bag. By implementing an "eye-to-hand" camera configuration for enhanced spatial awareness, the open-source Pi0 model —developed by Physical Intelligence on Google Cloud infrastructure— achieved an initial 85% baseline success rate in these early lab environments, providing a strong foundation for the next phase of rigorous training and safety refinement. Because vision-language-action (VLA) models connect language directly to physical movement, astronauts could direct the robotic system flexibly via standard English text prompts. Space: the ultimate edge-computing environment Processing these complex tasks requires significant computing power, which presents another hurdle: space is the ultimate edge computing environment. Spacecraft cannot rely on continuous connections to Earth-based data centers. To solve this, the Google team harnessed Google Cloud G4 instances to rapidly train the underlying models, fine-tuning the 4-billion parameter Pi0 model in just 2.5 hours. Crucially, they demonstrated that the fine-tuned models can then operate locally on compact, energy-efficient edge devices. Over the last two years, the team tested approximately 15 different edge computing devices to find ones that run efficiently on lightweight, low-power hardware required for future Mars missions. Pioneering the future of crew safety and space exploration Looking ahead, the ultimate goal is to build a robotic system that can execute a variety of tasks via simple voice instructions, under the astronauts’ direct supervision and command. For instance, the robot might be directed to assist with routine health monitoring—such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds—under the strict guidance of a human crew medical officer. This ensures astronauts receive the physical assistance they might not be able to perform by themselves, without ever replacing human decision-making. This collaboration between Google Public Sector and NASA can help pave the way for increasingly difficult missions that push the bounds of scientific discovery. title: Easy to integrate, compliant by design: Bringing the Swiss Franc to Google Cloud Universal Ledger
raw_text: Every day, countless financial transactions are interrupted by slow, expensive, and inflexible conventional payment systems. As a result, public commercial stablecoins like Tether, USDC, and PayPal USD have become increasingly popular by making it easy to move money efficiently with instant, 24/7 blockchain settlement. Yet major regulated banks have largely kept such transactions at arm’s length; for these financial institutions, reserve-backed public stablecoins present numerous risks, including strict capital and liquidity requirements and unmanageable regulatory and operational uncertainty. Indeed, banks don't want to adopt existing stablecoins. Instead, they need the speed and efficiency of tokenized currency built on the trusted economic foundations they’ve nurtured over years or even decades in business. That’s why many are now turning to Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL). Rather than channeling public stablecoins, GCUL provides the secure infrastructure banks need to issue and settle tokenized deposits. That brings real-time, 24/7 programmable payments into commercial bank money while satisfying regulators and without disrupting core banking operations. For many banks, this is a compelling vision, but adopting new payment technology and integrating it with core banking systems can seem to bank CTOs like a daunting undertaking. That’s particularly true as they face mounting demands for the engineering resources that keep their businesses running while also striving to stay compliant with new regulations. But with a blockchain purpose-built for financial services like GCUL, this is anything but a herculean task. Looking to expand its offerings for an increasingly global clientele, Switzerland’s Crypto Finance Group wanted to show it could deploy payment innovations like this in just weeks. That was its inspiration for launching a digital payments infrastructure pilot that enabled instant account-to-account transfers between customers of two Swiss banks on the GCUL network. The pilot, which was designed to operate within one of the world's most demanding financial security frameworks, provided a blueprint for how any commercial bank can build on Google Cloud technology to fundamentally modernize its payment operations. Pain points in today's payments landscape In recent years, there’s been a marked proliferation of tokenized payment methods. But stablecoins have transformed this previously niche technology, by effectively resolving some of traditional finance’s most enduring pain points, such as weekend transfer blackouts, direct transfers without correspondent banks, and fast settlement rails. Stablecoins also limit the frustrations caused by opaque cross-border transactions, where fragmented compliance checks can leave legitimate payments in extended and unexplained limbo and without a path to clear or timely resolution. Still, commercial banks have been reluctant to offer popular reserve-backed stablecoins from permissionless blockchains to their customers despite their retail popularity. That’s because they come with numerous challenges to smooth and secure operations: an uncertain regulatory status, compliance issues around anonymous accounts, gas fees , and the scalability limitations of layer 1 blockchain technology. But perhaps banks’ biggest concerns about stablecoins is that they create a problematic economic disconnect — giving customers access to reserve-backed stablecoins reduces reserves and, as a recent McKinsey study found, banks’ ability to lend. As a result, many banks are trying to figure out how to offer their customers the benefits of stablecoins — high speed, low cost, 24/7 availability, and programmability — without introducing problems often associated with existing reserve-backed stablecoins, such as regulatory issues, poor throughput performance, negative influence on bank reserves, and potentially no yield participation. Solution proposal Realizing this vision means modernized payments architectures must seamlessly and instantly enable individuals and institutions to transfer bank-held assets to accounts at any target bank. Orchestrating this shared ecosystem requires central entities to establish the governing rulebook, enforce issuance limits, and manage network-wide settlement parameters. During its pilot, Crypto Finance assumed this role, which within GCUL is known as the “currency operator.” In this position, Crypto Finance can configure the network for either instant or deferred settlement. This choice is analogous to traditional banking: instant settlement acts like real-time gross settlement, where transactions settle individually and immediately and require high liquid reserves. In contrast, deferred settlement operates like netting, where payments are accumulated and offset and only periodically settle the net difference. For the pilot, Crypto Finance chose to adopt deferred settlement, in which GCUL manifests capital efficiency. In this way, clients enjoy instant transfers while banks conserve liquidity through periodic settlement. Concept validation To demonstrate instant, bi-directional account-to-account transfers on GCUL, Crypto Finance orchestrated a pilot with two digital token issuers, a Swiss digital asset bank, and a Swiss B2B transaction bank. Crypto Finance established the rulebook for interactions between the participant banks, such as interbank settlement, integration with traditional SIC payment rails, and AML/compliance protocols. Although some backend steps still needed manual intervention, Crypto Finance’s pilot proved that fully automated, cross-institution integration is feasible and established a generalized architecture that can scale to virtually any asset class. Robustness and performance A temporary pilot is one thing; moving into live client transactions carrying legal liability brings a whole new set of operational challenges. Live payment rails are considered critical infrastructure that demands security and availability. GCUL addresses these needs through redundancy between geographically distributed nodes operating on an enterprise-grade consensus model, ensuring reliability. Deploying client workloads on Google Cloud provides that enterprise-grade foundation and allows financial institutions to pair the highly resilient GCUL network with secure-by-design infrastructure, encryption at rest and in transit, and robust access controls that satisfy many of banks’ common regulatory, privacy, and data sovereignty mandates. While some banks may consider integrating their systems with fully public and permissionless blockchains, this approach introduces severe regulatory hurdles, anonymity risks, unpredictable gas fees, and low throughput. These are all roadblocks that in the past would have significantly delayed the pilot or rendered it a non-starter. Ease of integration The pilot's implementation, with systems integration completed in under three months, was compartmentalized across dedicated Google Cloud projects per participant. The currency operator, Crypto Finance, connected specialized components to a dedicated GCUL API. The first was a role admin service that controls account managers and token managers on the network. Next, it implemented a settlement registry to record when periodic off-ledger settlement between participant banks has occurred once a predefined threshold is reached. Finally, a cloud key management service (KMS) stored the currency operator keys to sign transactions. At the same time, participant banks connected their core banking systems to their own GCUL API instances. But these participant banks don’t need a large Google Cloud footprint. Instead, they can connect to GCUL nodes via Remote Procedure Call from their existing on-premise deployments and manage private key material through solutions other than KMS. Regardless of the setup, transactions are seamlessly routed to the shared global GCUL nodes. Whether GCUL is exposed to a bank’s client or used merely as a bank backend is entirely at the integrating institution’s discretion. The banks participating in the pilot chose the latter, utilizing the ledger to upgrade their backend infrastructure. With GCUL under the hood, they improved intra-day transaction performance and provided customers with the user experience they were already accustomed to. Regulatory compliance and governance by design To join the Swiss Franc currency network on GCUL, participants must have regulatory licenses that let them perform third-party transfers and issue commercial bank money. Crucially, features like token and account management are not rigid network-wide limitations. Instead, they rely entirely on the currency operator and its specific rulebook. This standardizes fees, limits, settlement times, and technical configurations. Managing counterparty risk is central to this governance. Rather than relying on unscalable bilateral agreements or complex clearinghouse default waterfalls, GCUL mitigates risk through these currency operator-enforced issuance limits. It’s important to distinguish GCUL’s broader feature set from the concrete pilot setup. In the pilot, both participating banks operated with conservative initial limits based on their credit ratings in order to safely prove the architecture. But beyond the pilot, the network frees up capital by periodically netting outstanding obligations, which frees banks from having to fund and settle every transaction. Looking ahead, risk management can be further innovated. One clever future enhancement would be to allow participants to dynamically increase their issuance limits by committing digital assets as collateral in segregated accounts, using solutions like Crypto Finance’s AnchorNote pledging solution. These assets could then be used to instantly settle outstanding street-side obligations, virtually eliminating counterparty risk without tying up traditional liquidity reserves. The future While Crypto Finance’s pilot was designed to focus on domestic commercial bank money transfers in Switzerland, GCUL's programmable architecture and high-performance smart contract language, GCULpy, are paving the way for deeper innovation. As institutions like Crypto Finance scale their use of GCUL, the network can expand to support real-time cross-currency settlement, automated foreign exchange, and dynamic collateral management involving tokenized digital assets. And looking further ahead, this infrastructure has laid the groundwork for next-generation financial services that range from point-of-sale payments to autonomous, AI-driven agentic payments. The pilot proved that deploying high-performance, blockchain-based payment rails doesn’t mean compromising on strict regulatory compliance or core banking stability. By combining the high-throughput of GCUL with a secure, API-driven integration architecture, commercial banks can offer stablecoin-like speed to their customers while seamlessly preserving their capital efficiency. Ultimately, this compliant-by-design approach targets the operational bottlenecks of traditional finance while mitigating the inherent risks and complexities of public blockchains. title: Unifying enterprise context and semantics: LookML in Knowledge Catalog is now GA
raw_text: As enterprises go from experimental AI agent prototypes to using them in production, data teams are realizing that access to data is not the same as understanding that data. To help bridge that gap, today, we are announcing the general availability (GA) of LookML semantic language indexing in Knowledge Catalog for Looker Core on Google Cloud . To answer a complex business question accurately, an AI agent needs context — table schemas, data lineage, governance policies, business definitions, etc.. However, context is not a monolith; knowing where data lives is very different from knowing how to calculate metrics with it. In the enterprise, teams often conflate broad organizational context (usually in the form of metadata from structured and unstructured documents) with deterministic business semantics (the exact SQL formulas, join paths, and filtering rules that define metrics like net revenue or churn), assuming that a single data catalog or a business intelligence (BI) tool handling both enterprise-wide asset discovery and precise metric calculation. In reality, no one tool can carry the entire load for agentic AI, as enterprise agents require both organizational context and deterministic business semantics. In Google Cloud environments, those are provided by Knowledge Catalog and LookML: Broad enterprise context with Knowledge Catalog: Agents need a unified context graph that aggregates metadata across structured tables and unstructured documents. Through Knowledge Catalog, agents discover assets, inspect data quality, trace end-to-end lineage, respect column-level privacy tags, and surface corporate policy documents. The context graph tells an agent what data exists, how it is governed, and how it is connected. Deterministic mathematical semantics with LookML: What a catalog does not author on its own is how the numbers are computed. Describing a table is not the same as defining how tables join or how metrics are calculated. Looker's modeling language, LookML, encodes production-tested semantic logic — multi-grain join protections, conditional filters, and exact KPI formulas — so agents don't guess SQL math at runtime. With this native integration, the LookML business logic that powers your trusted BI reporting is automatically indexed into Knowledge Catalog — giving Gemini Enterprise and custom AI agents both enterprise-wide discovery and deterministic BI semantics. Why a context graph needs deterministic semantics When an LLM agent connects directly to raw database tables — even when armed with basic table descriptions or a business glossary — it still has to infer mathematical relationships on the fly. Without explicit semantic rules, agents routinely fall into two traps: Metric definition drift: Standard text-to-SQL agents can invent conflicting formulas for foundational KPIs like net revenue or customer acquisition cost, failing to apply domain-specific accounting rules (such as recognizing revenue only when order_status = 'Complete' or prorating annual contracts across active service days). Naive join fan-outs: Complex schemas often contain one-to-many (1:N) and zero-to-many (0:N) relationships across invoices, line items, and refunds. Without pre-modeled join relationships and symmetric aggregation rules, agent-generated SQL can multiply rows and inflate financial totals. Knowledge Catalog and Looker solve this together, enabling you to model once in LookML and access those semantics everywhere across Google Cloud's AI ecosystem. Knowledge Catalog enforces semantic math when that logic is defined in a semantic modeling tool; LookML provides a mature, production-proven language for defining those exact mathematical relationships. What's new: LookML in Knowledge Catalog Previously, catalog integrations only captured shallow, file-level pointers and basic dashboard inventories. With this release, LookML's deterministic semantics become a first-class layer in the Knowledge Catalog context graph. An agent that finds a metric in the graph now also finds its exact definition, its join path, and its lineage back to source tables — in the same place, under the same governance. Synchronization is always on by default with no action required from end users, and with live sync, any update pushed to production LookML is reflected in Knowledge Catalog in near-real-time so agents operate on the freshest business logic. Because this metadata is indexed directly into Knowledge Catalog by default, it is immediately available to Gemini Enterprise , without custom agent code or separate catalog data stores. When connected to Knowledge Catalog, Gemini Enterprise uses built-in read-only skills and hybrid search to look up technical schemas, business glossaries, and indexed LookML logic in a single step, passing that rich context directly to your federated BigQuery connector to generate accurate SQL. (For developers building custom agents, the same context bundles are also accessible via the LookupContext API.) Knowledge Catalog now captures and links the following entity levels across Looker Core on Google Cloud: LookML models (looker-model): Captures descriptive metadata, database connection routing, include hierarchies, data validation tests (assert), and parent-child EntryLinks mapping models to their associated Explores, Views, and LookML dashboards. LookML Explores (looker-explore): Indexes full relational join logic (type, sql_on, relationship cardinality such as many_to_one fan-out protection, foreign_key, required_joins, and sql_where) as Schema-Join relationships. It also captures mandatory filter guardrails (always_filter, access_filter), inherited dimensions and measures, and predefined starter queries that help agents and analysts overcome the cold-start problem. LookML Views and fields (looker-view): Extracts column-level compiled LookML SQL expressions (for example, ${total_revenue} / NULLIF(${count}, 0)), primary keys, dimension group timeframes, field synonyms, and derived table transformation logic (including SQL and native derived tables, partition keys, and cluster keys). Dashboards, Looks, and tiles (looker-dashboard, looker-dashboard-element, looker-look): Catalogs both UI-created and LookML-defined dashboards and visualization tiles, complete with dashboard filters, chart types, ownership, and usage statistics. Users in Knowledge Catalog are able to see table- and column-level lineage from underlying BigQuery tables all the way to individual dashboard tiles, allowing data engineers to evaluate schema changes proactively, before disruptions occur. Looker Core on Google Cloud automatically indexes resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, lineage, and dashboards directly into Knowledge Catalog. Three patterns for data agents Bringing LookML into Knowledge Catalog gives Gemini Enterprise (and your broader agent ecosystem) a single place to retrieve both broad organizational context and governance from Knowledge Catalog and explicit mathematical relationships and SQL definitions authored in LookML. To see the impact of combining these two layers in Gemini Enterprise, compare how three architectures handle a complex cross-domain prompt: "What was our total revenue last fiscal quarter by product category, and which regional promotional policy limits apply?" Agent architecture System mechanics Data logic and governance resolution User experience and token efficiency Pattern 1: Baseline database agent Data warehouse only Direct LLM writing raw SQL against warehouse tables with no semantic or catalog context. Ungoverned and non-deterministic Has no visibility into data quality, PII tags, or corporate documents, and guesses SQL metric logic blindly — assuming a standard January fiscal calendar, summing uncompleted orders, and exposing restricted customer PII. Fragile and high-risk Prone to schema hallucinations, fails on questions requiring unstructured policy context, and burns tokens in multi-turn SQL debugging loops. Pattern 2: Context-grounded agent Knowledge Catalog without indexed semantics Gemini Enterprise or another agent platform uses Knowledge Catalog to look up table descriptions, glossary terms, PII governance aspects, and unstructured policy PDFs, then writes SQL via the warehouse connector. Context-grounded, but lacks semantic SQL logic Enforces Knowledge Catalog governance and retrieves unstructured promotional policy rules, but lacks semantic definitions for SQL metrics and table relationships. This approach can miss conditional accounting rules (like order_status = 'Complete') or cause join fan-outs across multi-grain tables. Governed discovery, inconsistent math Solves asset discovery, compliance, and unstructured context, but still suffers from text-to-SQL calculation drift and multi-turn SQL retries. Pattern 3: Context + semantic-grounded agent Knowledge Catalog + Looker Core on Google Cloud with indexed LookML Gemini Enterprise or another agent platform connects to Knowledge Catalog enriched with indexed LookML metadata, automatically retrieving both broad catalog context and LookML join paths and field formulas to ground its SQL generation. Governed context plus semantic SQL definitions Enforces Knowledge Catalog PII aspects, retrieves unstructured policy PDFs, and grounds its SQL in LookML's exact mathematical definitions indexed in Knowledge Catalog, applying status = 'Complete', the May–July fiscal calendar, and predefined join conditions across warehouse tables. Accurate and token-efficient: Pre-mapped LookML join blueprints and compiled SQL expressions replace guessing, prevent join fan-outs, reduce SQL retry loops, and let the agent point users to relevant Looker dashboards and Explores. When you follow pattern 3 and pair Knowledge Catalog with Looker's semantic layer in an enterprise agent workflow, the agent moves from guessing at raw SQL to a governed, two-stage execution flow: Context and governance discovery in Knowledge Catalog: Before touching any data, the agent searches Knowledge Catalog, verifies that the thelook_ecommerce LookML model is gold-certified, checks column-level governance tags, and maps the prompt to exact LookML dimensions and measures, converting natural language into structured business intent. Deterministic semantic execution: Rather than having the LLM invent SQL on the fly, the agent grounds its SQL in LookML's exact mathematical definitions indexed in Knowledge Catalog and returns trusted, repeatable figures. Alongside the answer, the agent returns an interactive Open in Looker Explore link with the exact measures and filters pre-populated, letting users slice, dice, and inspect row-level line items in a single click. Side-by-side comparison of a baseline agent querying BigQuery directly (left), which guesses at raw SQL and fiscal dates, versus an agent governed by Knowledge Catalog and Looker (right), which applies indexed LookML definitions and returns an interactive "Open in Looker Explore" link. Scaling agents for BI and the enterprise A common question from data leaders is: "If we use Looker Conversational Analytics, when do we use an enterprise agent grounded in Knowledge Catalog?" The two experiences are designed for complementary jobs across your organization: Looker Conversational Analytics is your dedicated BI assistant: When business users are working inside BI workflows and asking questions scoped to a focused set of curated Looker Explores, Conversational Analytics delivers immediate, self-service data exploration and visualization directly within Looker. Knowledge Catalog + Looker powers your enterprise-wide agents: When users ask questions in Gemini Enterprise across federated Data Cloud sources like BigQuery, they often span structured tables, BI metrics, and unstructured documents. Enabling Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise gives the assistant built-in skills to dynamically discover relevant semantics across hundreds of LookML models, pass indexed LookML join definitions, metric SQL formulas, and starter queries to the BigQuery connector to prevent join hallucinations, and enforce centralized governance aspects and IAM. Getting started Because Looker Core on Google Cloud, Knowledge Catalog, and Gemini Enterprise are natively integrated, you can connect your existing LookML business logic to your enterprise AI assistant in just a few clicks, with no custom agent code required. To start discovering Looker semantics and grounding your agents: Confirm first-party metadata indexing is enabled for Looker Core on Google Cloud. This is enabled by default for new instances, with no additional charge for storing Looker technical metadata. Once enabled, metadata synchronization into Knowledge Catalog is always on by default (across both initial indexing and ongoing live updates). Enable the Cloud Dataplex API and Data Lineage API in your project and grant users the required view roles (roles/dataplex.viewer, roles/looker.schemaViewer, and roles/datalineage.viewer) to have your resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, join paths, and dashboards automatically sync into Knowledge Catalog. Enable Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise . When you attach a BigQuery (or Spanner, Cloud SQL, or AlloyDB) data store in federated query mode to your Gemini Enterprise app, the Knowledge Catalog integration is enabled automatically. You can also turn it on or off at any time in the Google Cloud console by opening your Gemini Enterprise app, navigating to Configurations > Assistant, toggling on Enable Knowledge Catalog, and clicking Save and publish. Ask questions . Gemini Enterprise connects to Knowledge Catalog using end-user credentials, meaning users only discover and query data assets they have IAM permission to view (such as roles/bigquery.dataViewer). Behind the scenes, the assistant automatically looks up your indexed LookML definitions, join logic, and starter queries in Knowledge Catalog and passes them to your federated connector to deliver accurate, governed answers. To dive deeper, read the Manage Looker Core on Google Cloud with Knowledge Catalog documentation and learn how to Connect to Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise . To build a more customized experience, explore our hands-on ADK agent codelab on GitHub .
summary: As enterprises go from experimental AI agent prototypes to using them in production, data teams are realizing that access to data is not the same as understanding that data. To help bridge that gap, today, we are announcing the general availability (GA) of LookML semantic language indexing in Knowledge Catalog for Looker Core on Google Cloud . To answer a complex business question accurately, an AI agent needs context — table schemas, data lineage, governance policies, business definitions, etc.. However, context is not a monolith; knowing where data lives is very different from knowing how to calculate metrics with it.
