title: MWC Doha aims to position Middle East as global hub for AI and digital infrastructure
raw_text:
MWC Doha, which returns to Qatar for its second edition on 8-10 November, aims to establish the Middle East as a central player in global discussions around connectivity, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure, according to Jawad Abbassi, head of MENA at the GSMA.

While MWC has traditionally been associated with Barcelona and Shanghai, Abbassi said Doha offers a strategic location from which to connect markets across Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Europe, putting more than five billion people within reach.

“MWC Doha delivers a full-scale MWC experience, on par with Barcelona and Shanghai,” he said.

The event also provides a platform for governments to connect national digital strategies with private sector investment. Qatar National Vision 2030 and Saudi Vision 2030, alongside similar programmes across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), are driving investment in technology, infrastructure and economic diversification.

“MWC Doha’s role is to be that meeting point for the leaders and decision-makers that deliver those visions, and gives the Middle East and North Africa its own home within the GSMA’s global MWC series,” Abbassi said.

This year’s event coincides with the International Telecommunication Union’s (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference (PP-26), bringing digital policymakers from more than 190 ITU member states to Doha alongside industry leaders and technology innovators. The GSMA sees the combination as an opportunity to bring policy discussions and industry priorities closer together.

From 5G roll-out to enterprise value

Across the Middle East, telecoms markets are moving beyond the initial deployment of 5G towards more advanced networks and new commercial opportunities. Abbassi identified the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait as among the world’s most advanced 5G markets, with operators progressing towards 5G Standalone, 5G-Advanced and reduced-capability (RedCap) technologies.

The next phase will depend on how effectively businesses translate connectivity investments into measurable economic outcomes. GSMA research projects that enterprise spending on digital transformation across MENA will average 9.8% of revenues between 2025 and 2030. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE are among the world’s top seven digital transformation spenders, according to Abbassi.

However, expanding network coverage alone will not be sufficient to realise the region’s digital ambitions. Although 96% of the MENA population lived within mobile broadband coverage, only 49% were using mobile internet by the end of 2023, he said. The difference highlights what the industry calls the mobile internet usage gap: people who live within coverage areas but do not use mobile internet services.

Closing that gap will require greater affordability, digital skills and locally relevant content, Abbassi said. Doing so could extend the benefits of connectivity to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), healthcare, education and underserved communities.

Telecoms operators take on a broader role in AI

As governments and businesses invest in AI, cloud computing and datacentres, telecoms operators are increasingly positioning themselves as infrastructure providers beyond traditional connectivity.

AI services require access to data, cloud capacity, edge infrastructure and reliable networks. Operators are therefore investing in the infrastructure needed to support increasingly data-intensive workloads, while also applying AI to their own network operations.

Abbassi pointed to du’s datacentre partnership with Microsoft and e&’s agreements with Huawei, Ericsson, Nokia and Intel to apply AI across its mobile networks as examples of how regional operators are expanding their role in the technology ecosystem.

Network application programming interfaces (APIs) represent another opportunity. Through the GSMA’s Open Gateway initiative, operators can expose standardised network capabilities to developers, making it easier to build services that use telecoms infrastructure without negotiating separate arrangements in every market.

For developers and enterprise technology teams, the initiative could simplify access to network capabilities and create opportunities for services that depend on connectivity, security and network intelligence. The wider challenge will be turning infrastructure investment into scalable services and business models that deliver value beyond the telecoms sector.

Digital sovereignty and global partnerships

The region’s ambitions to develop sovereign AI capabilities and strengthen control over critical digital infrastructure are also reshaping technology investment.

Governments are seeking greater control over strategic assets, including data, computing capacity and semiconductor supply chains, while continuing to rely on international technology partners.

Abbassi explained that these objectives need not conflict. “Global collaboration has been a key driver of progress in the mobile and digital technology sectors, and the GSMA advocates for open markets and policies that support cross-border cooperation alongside each country’s own digital ambitions,” he said.

He cited Qatar and the UAE joining Pax Silica, a US-aligned initiative focused on semiconductor and AI supply chains, alongside their investments in domestic AI infrastructure.

Qatar Investment Authority’s $2bn expansion of its venture capital programme, aimed at attracting global funds and AI startups to Doha, is another example of the country’s efforts to combine sovereign investment with international participation.

For technology leaders, the balance between sovereignty and collaboration will have implications for cloud strategy, infrastructure sourcing, data governance and access to advanced AI capabilities.

Abbassi said global partnerships would remain critical to scaling AI responsibly, with open standards and predictable regulatory environments helping countries pursue national priorities while maintaining international cooperation.

AI, intelligent economies and connected infrastructure

MWC26 Doha’s programme is organised around three themes: AI in Action, Intelligent Economies and Connected Infrastructure.

AI in Action will examine how telecoms companies are turning embedded intelligence into practical outcomes. Intelligent Economies will focus on the policies and partnerships needed to build competitive and inclusive digital economies. Connected Infrastructure will explore how next-generation networks can deliver performance, resilience and security at scale.

Dedicated summits will cover sovereign AI and national digital strategy, intelligent datacentres, agentic AI, open telecoms AI, future networks, and satellite and non-terrestrial networks (NTNs).

The return of the GSMA Ministerial Programme and the inclusion of 4YFN Doha, the GSMA’s startup showcase, are intended to broaden the event’s reach across government, established technology companies and emerging businesses.

The agenda reflects the increasingly interconnected nature of the region’s digital transformation priorities. AI adoption depends on computing infrastructure and connectivity, while the commercial success of those investments relies on enterprise demand, regulatory frameworks and access to skills and capital.

Turning regional ambition into partnerships

For the GSMA, success at MWC26 Doha will depend on building on the inaugural event and demonstrating sustained international interest in the region’s technology ambitions.

Abbassi identified two priorities: showcasing global interest in MENA’s digital future, and demonstrating why the region is positioned to help shape the future of connectivity, AI and digital infrastructure. For the wider technology ecosystem, he said the event should serve as a catalyst for collaboration, connecting policy priorities with industry investment and giving regional innovation greater international visibility.

“MWC Doha will continue to act as a meeting point and productivity catalyst where conversations become partnerships, policy priorities align with industry investment, and regional innovation gets showcased to a global audience,” Abbassi added.

title: Azure licensing lock-in limits choice
raw_text:
A survey of 410 software and cloud decision-makers in US businesses has found that organisations are putting off investment due to Microsoft software licensing costs.

Respondents reported finding that costs are higher when using a cloud provider other than Microsoft Azure to host Microsoft software. According to the Coalition for Fair Software Licensing, this demonstrates that customers are being steered to Azure through financial penalty rather than merit, and workloads are being locked out of the cloud.

Over half of affected businesses (56%) have increased prices to cover the cost. The same number have also cut other spending, while 33% have slowed hiring.

The survey also reported that 83% claimed Microsoft’s licensing rules have a meaningful impact on their choice of cloud provider. In fact, 18% said they have never considered a competing provider, while 61% of organisations that did look at alternatives still selected Azure to avoid fees.

Ryan Triplette, executive director of the Coalition for Fair Software Licensing, said: “Microsoft’s customers are telling us the system is broken. Businesses are being steered to Azure by financial penalties rather than by merit. They are passing the costs on to their own customers and delaying [investment in] the AI [artificial intelligence] tools they need to compete. Some are choosing not to migrate to the cloud at all, rather than incur the costs associated with Microsoft’s licences to do so.”

Triplette said the survey showed that the closer a decision-maker is to Microsoft’s licensing practices, the more urgently they want regulators to step in. He urged regulators to take note: “What happens next matters to every American business, and every consumer paying more because of Microsoft’s anti-competitive licensing practices.” 

Under the UK’s Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, a company designated as having strategic market status (SMS) has substantial and entrenched market power and a position of strategic significance in respect of a digital activity.

In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has been investigating whether Microsoft should be designated with SMS with regard to its business software, which includes its Office productivity suite, Windows and SQL Server.

Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA, said: “Business software and cloud services underpin workplaces across the UK, from small firms to vital public services. The evidence shows Microsoft has a long-standing and significant presence in the UK’s business software market.

“Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives.

“We’re now consulting on whether to designate Microsoft with strategic market status. If we do, our focus would be on promoting competition and giving businesses greater freedom to choose and combine products in business software.”

Microsoft has also been battling with European regulators.

In 2023, the European Commission began a formal investigation to assess whether Microsoft may have breached European Union competition rules by tying or bundling its communication and collaboration product Teams to its popular suites for businesses Office 365 and Microsoft 365.

This led to changes to Microsoft licensing across the European Economic Area and Switzerland, where the company agreed to unbundle Teams from its Office suite.

title: TechEd 2026: SAP fronts tabular data model in space as it bids to make autonomous enterprise real
raw_text:
At SAP TechEd 2025 in Berlin, Philipp Herzig, chief technology officer of SAP, finished the opening keynote with a flourish in space. The supplier’s tabular data foundation model, RPT-2, is being deployed, with technology from HPE, aboard the International Space Station. RPT-1 [pronounced “rapid one”] was announced at TechEd last year. It functions like a large language model [LLM] that will predict the next word in a sentence, but for structured data, according to SAP. It is used to make predictions for business scenarios, such as delivery delays or payment risk.

“If we can run maintenance predictions in one of the most unforgiving environments, think what this means for our operations here on Earth,” said Herzig. “That’s AI [artificial intelligence] proven under pressure.”

In a blog post, Brenda Brown, the supplier’s chief marketing officer for SAP Business AI Platform and Joule, said: “SAP [has] announced the planned deployment of SAP-RPT, our tabular AI foundation model, on HPE Spaceborne Computer-2 aboard the International Space Station (ISS), one of the most significant edge compute validations of an enterprise AI model to date.”

She further said the model “makes predictions directly from structured data – even with some data missing – and without requiring the usual model training or fine-tuning. Running directly onboard the ISS on HPE Spaceborne Computer-2, it supports anomaly triage in real-time telemetry data, predicts issues before failures escalate, reconstructs missing sensor values based on historical data, and generates explainable mission-health reports for astronauts and ground teams.”

In a press statement, Herzig added: “The same trusted SAP-RPT model that powers global supply chains also can work in space.

“SAP’s deep-rooted, proven expertise has led to the International Space Station’s use of our tabular foundation model to predict potential mission-critical failures in orbit,” he said. “With SAP RPT and TabPFN from [SAP acquisition] Prior Labs, we bring the unique capabilities of tabular AI into the enterprise and across every frontier.”

The broad theme of TechEd is to put some flesh on the bones of the “autonomous enterprise” vision adumbrated at this year’s Sapphire conferences in Florida and Madrid.

Evolution

Florian Kunzke, SAP’s global director of artificial intelligence strategy, said in a pre-conference press briefing with international press: “We will see an evolution of our strategy so far, moving from the slides in our announcements at Sapphire into the productive environments of our customers, which is the hardest thing to do.”

The supplier is announcing enhancements to its Joule Studio and Joule Work technologies, and its Business AI Platform, including the tabular foundation model on board the space station. The supplier describes Joule Work as “a foundational capability within SAP’s AI suite that orchestrates complex business workflows, automates cross-functional tasks, and manages end-to-end operational processes autonomously across enterprise applications”.

SAP is also putting forward new tools to build AI agents and endeavouring to provide a “richer data and business context for those agents to reason with, and strengthened governance controls to run them responsibly across the enterprise”.

Herzig said, in the main statement for the event: “SAP TechEd has always been where builders shape what comes next,” he said, adding that this was the 30th event of its kind. “This year, we are showing how we are moving from AI learning your business to running it. Joule Work is where you put your intent and get work done, in one experience across the entire SAP landscape and beyond. That is the shift we are delivering at scale.

“Everything underneath runs on SAP Business AI Platform, delivering faster time to value, business understanding, higher accuracy, enterprise-readiness that is secure, governed and compliant, and a unique context layer built on over 50 years of process and industry expertise, encoded into every agent action.”

At last week’s SAP AI Tour event in Birmingham, Manos Raptopoulos, global president of customer success, said in the keynote session: “AI means technology is now back in the boardroom, but is it delivering business value? When LLMs can’t do Arithmetic, 90% accuracy is not good enough for businesses.”

He argued that grounding SAP’s AI technology Joule in a “context layer” made possible by customers’ use of the supplier’s enterprise resource planning over many years “reduces hallucinations by 89%”, adding that specific business knowledge, semantic richness and governance are what AI needs to deliver business value for SAP customers.

In an interview with Computer Weekly, Raptopoulos said that when it comes to getting business value from AI, “the first layer is the intelligence layer, which is your generative AI model, LLM, call it whatever. There is another layer, which is the context layer, and context here is twofold. One is the context of the system – when it comes at least to our own system, it’s the Knowedge Graph, as we call it, or the ontology, as some other people call it, but it’s also the context of the company, which we call company memory in terms of, “So how do we do things around here?”

“To get to what we call the autonomous enterprise, every customer is at a point A, and they have to go to point B,” he said. “There are certain customers that are more advanced on that journey, and every customer is somehow unique, but they are very much aware of that journey, of that transformation that they need to do.”

At TechEd, the supplier is announcing capabilities for Joule Work, said to help make AI agents be more effective at handling complex business processes via open protocols including Agent2Agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP). 

It talks about “agentic thinking capabilities that plan and orchestrate the steps assistants and agents need to reliably complete complex, multi-step business workflows across SAP landscapes”.

The supplier is also trumpeting master data management capabilities provided by recent acquisition Reltio and data lake capabilities proffered by another recent acquisition, Dremio. That is said to have native support for Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris, plus a high-performance, federated query engine that will enable unified data access without moving or copying the data. 

It is also announcing an expansion of its relationship with Databricks, whose CEO, Ali Ghodsi, had a message for the conference reaffirming its work with SAP.

title: Why measuring your public cloud carbon footprint is so hard
raw_text:
If a business wants to understand the carbon cost of its public cloud use, it should be able to ask a straightforward question – what emissions did our activity generate?

The answer is rarely straightforward. It depends what the provider measures, how emissions are divided between customers, which electricity accounting method is used and what sits outside the calculation. Establishing whether those emissions have fallen introduces another layer of complexity. Deciding what can credibly be offset depends on understanding both.

In my view, the fundamental difficulty is the distance between responsibility and visibility. Businesses are expected to account for the environmental impact of services they buy, while much of the evidence needed to do so sits with someone else.

Public cloud customers purchase access to computing resources. They do not own the infrastructure, directly measure its electricity consumption or control how it is replaced. They rely on their provider to translate a complex physical operation into a figure they can use.

That figure can be valuable. But we need to understand what it represents before building environmental claims around it.

Shared infrastructure and reporting gaps

Shared infrastructure is the first challenge. A server can support multiple customers, with storage, networking, cooling and other services shared across an even wider estate. Emissions therefore have to be allocated. Detailed methods can use measured energy consumption, resource reservations and hourly usage, but the customer’s footprint remains an attributed share of a larger system. It is not a direct reading from a meter attached to their business.

Allocation is unavoidable. The important questions are whether the method is transparent, whether it reflects the resources consumed and whether it is consistent enough to support meaningful comparisons.

Reporting frequency creates a further gap. A monthly total may help a sustainability team complete its reporting, without helping an IT team establish which decision changed its emissions. It can conceal variation between workloads and between different times of day, even where the underlying calculation uses more detailed data. Monthly customer reporting already exists, but a reporting total and an operational decision tool serve different purposes.

This matters because measurement should help businesses act. If we cannot connect the number to decisions about capacity, storage or processing, its usefulness is limited.

Scopes, grids and moving baselines

There is also the question of whose emissions we are counting. Electricity purchased to operate a cloud provider’s data centre generally falls within the provider’s Scope 2. For the customer buying the service, the associated emissions generally sit within Scope 3, as part of its supply chain. Moving infrastructure into the cloud can therefore change where emissions appear in a customer’s inventory. That change does not, by itself, establish that fewer emissions have occurred.

I think this is an important test for any migration claim. Has the environmental impact reduced, or has it moved outside the part of the organisation’s footprint that receives the most attention?

Electricity accounting adds another complication. Location-based figures reflect the electricity mix of the grid that serves a facility. Market-based figures reflect qualifying contractual arrangements for electricity purchases. A renewable electricity claim based on annual matching does not establish that every workload was powered by carbon-free electricity at every hour. Buyers need to understand which basis supports the figure they are being given.

Without that explanation, two figures can look comparable while answering different questions. A customer may also struggle to distinguish a reduction that results from lower consumption from one that results from changes in electricity purchasing.

Then we come to the baseline. To claim a reduction, an organisation needs a credible starting point and a consistent basis for comparison.

Cloud carbon calculations evolve as providers improve their data and methodologies. Those improvements can lead to historical figures being revised. That is a reason to maintain clear records of the calculation method, rather than assume that a dashboard total is permanently settled. Otherwise, businesses risk treating a change in measurement as a change in performance.

The activity being measured also needs to be comparable. If emissions fall because a business processes fewer transactions, that is different from delivering the same service more efficiently. Conversely, emissions per transaction may improve while total emissions increase as demand grows. Reporting absolute emissions and an appropriate measure of intensity would make these distinctions clearer. The Software Carbon Intensity specification offers a useful approach to relate operational and embodied emissions to a defined unit of activity.

Hardware lifecycles and AI hardware

Customers also have limited control over where and when emissions occur. Region selection can influence a workload’s footprint, but choices must accommodate requirements such as latency, resilience and data residency. Electricity carbon intensity varies geographically and over time – a regional average cannot explain every individual operating decision.

It is reasonable to expect customers to make informed choices. It is equally reasonable to expect providers to explain what customers can influence and what remains beyond their control.

My IT lifecycle perspective adds one further question: does the calculation adequately account for the equipment itself? Manufacturing and end-of-life emissions form part of a hardware footprint, and allocating them to a service requires assumptions about equipment lifespan and use. Some cloud methodologies include embodied emissions, so it would be wrong to suggest these are universally ignored. The issue is whether their coverage and assumptions are clear to the buyer.

AI infrastructure makes that scrutiny particularly relevant. More efficient accelerators can improve performance per unit of energy, but a sound assessment also considers manufacturing and the consequences of replacement. Customers need enough information to understand whether an apparent improvement covers the whole service lifecycle or only its electricity consumption.

The limits of offsetting

What does all this mean for offsetting?

An organisation can purchase credits against an estimated footprint. Uncertainty does not make that transaction impossible. It does, however, affect how confidently the organisation can claim that it has compensated for its emissions. Missing sources, unclear boundaries or revised calculations can change the quantity it is trying to address.

And measuring that quantity is only one part of the task. The credibility of the credits requires separate scrutiny. Purchasing them does not demonstrate that the cloud service itself has reduced its emissions. Offsets should be reported separately from the emissions inventory.

I would, therefore, put better measurement and practical reduction ahead of the claim. Buyers should ask providers to explain coverage, allocation methods, electricity accounting and methodology changes. Procurement, IT and sustainability teams should agree what evidence they need before committing to a public statement.

We should not wait for perfect data before removing unused resources or questioning unnecessary consumption. But we should be honest about the limits of the evidence.

Public cloud carbon is difficult to measure because infrastructure, information and control are shared unevenly between supplier and customer. The answer is greater transparency across that relationship. Until buyers can explain what their number includes, how it was calculated and why it changed, any claim about reducing or offsetting it needs to reflect that uncertainty.

If a business wants to understand the carbon cost of its public cloud use, it should be able to ask a straightforward question – what emissions did our activity generate?

The answer is rarely straightforward. It depends what the provider measures, how emissions are divided between customers, which electricity accounting method is used and what sits outside the calculation. Establishing whether those emissions have fallen introduces another layer of complexity. Deciding what can credibly be offset depends on understanding both.

In my view, the fundamental difficulty is the distance between responsibility and visibility.

title: Autumn Budget 2026: Healey sets out AI funding
raw_text:
Ahead of his autumn budget, chancellor of the exchequer John Healey has unveiled further investments in artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on risks to jobs and greater security.

His plans include £10m per year to improve the UK government’s understanding of how AI will reshape jobs and industry, and how the nation needs to prepare for it. The UK’s AI hardware capabilities will also receive £18m of support through a new UK Advanced Chip Design Academy for developing advanced chip-design skills. The academy aims to connect British research more directly with advanced semiconductor manufacturing, and to support the government’s drive towards re-industrialisation.

Healey wants to cut UK dependence on other countries to bolster security and resilience while supporting home-grown businesses and talent. Among the government’s plans are new investments in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh, alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester.

Discussing the investment boost in UK AI, Healey said: “AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit. I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.”

AI minister Kanishka Narayan discussed the need for technology sovereignty and strengthening cyber security defences: “As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future. That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on.”

Regarding technological sovereignty, Narayan said: “We cannot afford to rely entirely on technology built overseas. By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain’s industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country.”

Security minister Dan Jarvis added: “Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.” 

The investments include £165m for a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, of which £100m is being set aside for an AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) which will use AI for the detection and surveillance of biological threats.

The AIBL is also receiving £200m in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, plus partnerships with Google DeepMind and London-based AI life sciences pioneer Basecamp Research.

There is also an additional £120m investment in the AI Security Institute for building a shared scientific understanding by testing new AI systems and developing technical standards to ensure risks are mitigated.

The government plans to use agentic AI to improve the UK’s cyber defences through £60m of funding and a new £70m National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre where AI tools will be used to identify cyber vulnerabilities across UK critical infrastructure and the economy.

title: AI World: AI vulnerability surge brings change for Oracle’s cyber practice
raw_text:
With Microsoft’s regular Patch Tuesday updates now routinely comprising well over 1,000 vulnerabilities per month, Oracle has revealed that it too is picking up flaws in its products at a comparable rate – currently around 3,000 every quarter – which is forcing dramatic change when it comes to how it works with customer organisations on patching.

Speaking to reporters ahead of Oracle’s AI World opening, Gary Miller, the firm’s executive vice-president of customer success, said that since onboarding into the Glasswing artificial intelligence (AI) security programme earlier this year, Oracle has poured resources into addressing flaws in both its cloud and on-premise products using AI as a discovery mechanism.

“We’re using all of the different models to find vulnerabilities in our technology,” said Miller. “We’ll have one model that will find a vulnerability, we’ll have another check that it actually is a real one, and then we’ll have other models actually code and test the fix. Plus, these models don’t look for one way in. They string vulnerabilities together. They’re very complex [and] so we have to have a very complex response to that.”

Oracle’s patch cadence is also increasing – with the past seven days alone seeing about eight real-time patches dropping, said Miller.

“The problem is the speed with which bad actors find this stuff because they’re using the models as well, and they’re collaborating,” he said. “Are there going to be more one-off patches that everybody has to put out, like PHP? Yes.”

Interestingly, said Miller, not all of these vulnerabilities are being discovered by AI – indeed, the total number includes some that humans still found but the models brushed past. As a result, Oracle’s cyber experts are now tinkering around under the bonnet, actively fine-tuning the models to give them hints as to where trouble might be found.

“It’s now a combination of humans and frontier models that are finding issues and stringing things together,” he added. “It’s got pretty advanced.”

To help customers get used to life in this new normal, Oracle is ramping up what amounts to a large data-sharing exercise with its customers, with the intent of helping them understand exactly what Oracle products they are using, and which ones might be putting their security at risk. Alongside this is guidance on next steps and best practice.

“We use [OpenAI’s] Codex and we ran it against our whole installed base, and it came back for every customer with all the software they’ve got, the patch versions they’ve got, and the fixes they should apply,” said Miller. “That was within two days. And we gave that to customers. They can go and look at what they have [and] in many cases, customers didn’t know everything they had.”

On the patching side, Oracle is now making repeatable AI-powered testing capabilities available to customers that they can run against their systems as much as they like, while the supplier will work with those who may need or want additional safeguards at this stage to create digital twins of their Oracle environments to run patches against before deploying them into production.

“This is going to take time to flush out,” said Miller. “We have to work together as a community against bad actors. They’re also working as a community. They’re using AI tools. Our AI tools have to be better than they are. Their AI tools and our community has to be stronger than their community. This is going to be a team sport to get through this together.”

title: AI World: Oracle sets agents loose on Fusion Cloud apps
raw_text:
On the opening day of its annual AI World customer conference in Las Vegas, Nevada, Oracle unleashed a plethora of artificial intelligence (AI) innovations chiefly targeting its Fusion Cloud Applications suite, as CEO Mike Sicilia used his opening keynote to advance one vision of an Oracle-powered AI future.

Boasting of a “unique advantage” that has been decades in the making, Sicilia claimed that Oracle was well-placed to lead against four key metrics that will collectively enable AI to be truly effective in the enterprise.

First, he explained, AI Database will enable agents to access data, then the AI Data Platform will help them understand this data in the context of the wider business, while Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) will provide the high-performance infrastructure needed to run them. Finally, today’s Fusion announcements will enable them to work more effectively within business applications.

Sicilia’s AI doctrine would seem to hold that it is this final ‘pillar’ that is the most important – or at the very least the most visible to the everyday IT user. In his view, he explained to the keynote audience, the true measure of a successful AI deployment will ultimately be to make the underlying business application essentially invisible to the ordinary user.

According to Natalia Rachelson, senior vice-president of Oracle Applications, it is in this way that customers can realise immediate value because they will now clearly see tangible actions and outcomes from their agents.

“The mindset is changing. In the past, SaaS software helped record things, but people still had to direct and tell it what to do, people had to extract data and run reports,” said Rachelson.

“That paradigm is now shifting,” she told Computer Weekly. “We’re moving from Fusion just being a system of record to Fusion being an all-in-one system of record and system of outcomes.”

Underlying the suite of announcements Oracle made on the opening day of AI World is a new, open source Fusion Cloud Applications implementation service, which the supplier is making available through a public GitHub repository, and will supposedly make the setup and configuration process both machine-readable and executable entirely by AI agents.

The Oracle Fusion Setup and Configuration Registry (FSCR) will be built and maintained by Oracle and is designed to capture the supplier’s internal expertise on its own product suite as reusable AI skills that allow agents to plan, execute, test and validate directly in Fusion Cloud Applications, releasing humans to focus on other things, such as business transformation, process redesign and so on.

Part of the aim of FSCR is also to expand Oracle’s customer base by making it easier to get things up and running, said Rachelson, with the hope being that the free-of-charge service will induce users of its competitors to consider jumping ship to Fusion.

“Our goal is to get as many customers to Fusion as possible because that's where the AI value accrues for them,” she added.

Oracle said that its system integrator community will be free to extend the open foundation with methodologies, accelerators, automations and solutions of their own, and it will be actively pursuing these relationships with its channel partners.

The Claw

Alongside FSCR sits a range of new Fusion Agentic Applications powered by the recently launched Oracle Fusion Claw governed execution runtime, which is designed to allow Fusion Agentic Applications to run enterprise-scale work across multiple steps, different conditions, and large datasets, by marrying AI reasoning and deterministic computation.

The Claw-powered applications span multiple business functions, and 25 are being made available at launch across multiple Fusion products covering customer experience (CX), enterprise resource planning (ERP), human capital management (HCM), and supply chain and manufacturing (SCM). Functionality includes ledger, payroll, procurement, supply planning and workforce orchestration, among other things.

Finally, Oracle announced Fusion Companion and Fusion Agentic Home, two new overlay capabilities for Fusion Cloud Applications.

Fusion Companion will serve as an intelligent layer that can understand an organisation’s objectives and automatically takes the appropriate actions to achieve them – to Sicilia’s point about applications becoming somewhat less visible, Oracle says Companion users will “no longer need to know” what application to run or action to take, or even which agent to use.

Users will be able to access these capabilities via various supported AI tools – including the likes of ChatGPT – or through Agentic Home.

Agentic Home is designed to offer users a native AI experience inside Fusion Applications, letting them define their objectives, delegate work to agents and agentic applications, and track progress. Oracle said it would let organisations simplify employee workflows, make them more productive, better resolve edge cases and exceptions, and let agents doing the grunt work while humans focus on wider objectives or decisions that need their judgement – a process it refers to as governed delegation.

“This is about enterprise applications completely changing, and changing the way they [customers] operate,” said Rachelson. “From assisting people with the work, to taking on the work, we’re moving the work forward, and that is a huge takeaway.”

title: Capita ‘comprehensively failed’ on Civil Service pension artificial intelligence promise
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) promises made to the government by outsourcer Capita failed to materialise, providing the “biggest learning” from an independent audit into the failed civil service pension project.

The audit, by Grant Thornton, has also revealed major failings by Capita related to its promises to fix the scheme, which has left thousands of former civil servants in serious financial difficulties. Cabinet Office officials now have access to the relevant Capita systems and will be watching “every single day”, said government minister Sally Jameson.

In a parliamentary statement, Jameson, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, asserted that while Capita said it would be an AI-enabled pension scheme, that just was not the reality.

A government-commissioned independent audit of the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS), carried out by Grant Thornton, was received by the officials this month. It has laid bare Capita’s tech failings on the project it began working on in 2023, before taking control in December last year.

“We were promised ‘the most AI-enabled pensions service’. It is fair to say that Capita has comprehensively failed to deliver on that commitment,” Jameson told MPs. “The progress overall has been abysmal.”

The full audit report won’t be published, although MPs on the Public Accounts and Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs committees will see it.

Jameson said the report concluded that, “in a service whose success firmly relied on automation, Capita did not deliver the promised technology”.

She added that it also found Capita “had not been applying the right techniques to understand demand, productivity and capacity, and that it had not put in place effective mechanisms to detect and escalate failure”.

The minister also slammed Capita’s recovery plans: “It will not shock this House that the independent advisor’s report clearly shows that Capita’s rectification planning was wholly insufficient, their technology was weak and their ambition was falling well short of restoring the quality services that members deserve.”

The revelations contradict Capita claims made in February that a backlog of work left by the previous supplier, MYCSP, was the cause of the problems with the scheme since Capita took control in December. However, Jameson did also describe MYCSP’s performance as “abysmal”.

Government sees data

Jameson said that from now on, the government will have full access to Capita systems related to CSPS and full sight of the data.

“I agreed with Capita executives that Cabinet Office officials would work with Capita to develop a credible, workable and realistic recovery plan for which Capita alone will be held to account,” she said. “I can confirm that for the first time, Cabinet Office officials now have full access to capital systems and data.”

Jameson said Cabinet Office officials will now be watching Capita closely “every single day”.

“I will indeed be holding Capita’s feet to the fire every single step of the way on this rectification plan, and now that we have access to the Capita systems, we’ll be able to look every single day, as I know Cabinet Office officials are, to track that progress,” she added.

The government will now publish figures to allow the public and members of the scheme a clear view of performance. Members have questioned figures put out by Capita that appear to contradict what is happening to them.

“Every two weeks, we will be publishing the figures so people can see for themselves how Capita are performing,” said Jameson. “If they’re not up to scratch, I will return to this House.”

As revealed by Computer Weekly in September, the government set up a team to validate Capita data on the CSPS.

Insourcing debate

MPs repeatedly asked the minister about government plans to insource the scheme and other outsourced work.

“We absolutely must improve these services going forward, which is why we are exploring in-house models,” said Jameson. “We want to have a big wave of insourcing, because we can no longer be totally reliant on these companies that let us down time and again.”

“Following our previous commitments to Parliament, my officials have led an extensive programme of engagement with trade unions, practitioners and experts,” she said. “The evidence from those sessions was clear: restoring operational resilience and member trust must be the approach. I have instructed my officials to evaluate the viability of a range of future delivery options, including insourcing all core business operations.

“There are a number of different insourcing models in operation across the public sector that we will learn from, and we will consider which is the best approach to take for the civil service pension scheme and all the other schemes that it interacts with,” said Jameson, stressing, however, that insourcing decisions must wait until all former civil servants have their pensions paid.

“This government inherited a broken, outsourced administration,” she added. “We cannot replace a complex pension operation overnight, but let me be clear: this government will hold Capita to account and continue to apply the most stringent commercial levers, and we will not rest until every civil servant receives the pension they are entitled to.”

Fix first

Former civil servant Steve Tessier, who spent most of his career at the Ministry of Defence (MoD), as well as a spell on secondment at Nato, is still waiting for his pension after retiring last year.

“I don’t want more flannel: after waiting a year since retirement, I just want my money,” he said. “I’m concerned that the minister tried to shovel all of the blame onto Capita, ignoring the significant failure of governance by the cabinet office that allowed capita to wreak havoc.”

The Civil Service Pensions Campaigns Group, set up to support scheme members, welcomed the acknowledgement of the seriousness of the crisis and the need for independent verification.

“Capita’s claims that the contract is back on track have been largely discredited by the evidence and experiences of members still awaiting pensions, accurate quotations and even responses to MPs’ enquiries,” the group said.

“The reported failures surrounding technology and AI implementation raise serious questions about Capita’s management of the contract and the Cabinet Office’s oversight. We expect the Grant Thornton findings to be fully scrutinised, with clear accountability for what went wrong and the consequences for members.”

The group said questions over insourcing is a matter for Parliament and the government, but “any decision to bring the service back in-house must be supported by a robust, properly resourced transition plan that protects members from further disruption.

“Behind the statistics are ordinary civil servants suffering real financial and emotional hardship. Capita’s failures must also be taken into account when considering future government contracts. Members cannot afford another failed transition – they need their pensions paid accurately and on time, not further promises.”

Earlier this month, Capita said in a statement: “Capita recognises the need for continued service improvement, and we are implementing further automation along with stronger governance including improved management information. This will continue to improve operational output and member experience.

“Capita accepts that performance remains below the standards that scheme members and the government rightly expect. The remediation of CSPS remains the group’s top priority.”

title: EU makes progress towards PHP patching, UK lags behind
raw_text:
Organisations across the European Union (EU) are leading the charge to address the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, with patch rates hitting about 50% of exposed hosts in the Netherlands, the DACH – Austria, Germany and Switzerland – countries edging closer to 40%, and Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia and Finland hovering at around 30%.

However, British organisations are lagging behind, with barely a quarter of exposed hosts identified as located in the UK patched, while in the US things are moving even slower, with just under 20% of hosts now secured.

Globally, as of 12pm on Monday 26 October, 412,000 publicly accessible PHP hosts were patched, representing about 19% of the visible total.

This is according to live data provided by UK-based cyber startup Infrawatch, which has been tracking PHP2Shell patching rates since last week.

Meanwhile, evidence is stacking up that successful real-world compromises of PHP2Shell are now a reality. According to Bleeping Computer, a Perplexity researcher confirmed they observed remote code execution (RCE) exploiting PHP2Shell after setting up honeypots running a vulnerable version of PHP.

“The news that the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are now being successfully exploited in the wild isn’t surprising, but it adds even great urgency towards patching,” said Keith Simpson, group operations head at Converged Solutions Group, an Aberdeen-based managed services provider (MSP).

He added: “When major vulnerabilities are disclosed, threat actors move quickly to find ways to exploit them, and AI is now accelerating these efforts. The gap between disclosure and exploitation is shrinking and is often even shorter than the time organisations require to apply patches.

“While websites have been taken down across the globe, this is not a long-term solution. Many organisations will still not have patched, and they cannot overlook the threat. They must act today.”

This said, confirmation of successful PHP2Shell exploitation – even in a non-impactful honeypot environment – strongly suggests that threat actors have likely already compromised vulnerable real-world systems.

Over the coming days and weeks, this likely means that the opportunistic scanning activity seen to date will begin to morph into web shell deployment and credential theft, followed by brokered access sales to other cyber criminals, and ultimately, a spate of ransomware activity.

Business analysis firm Moodys said that observed exploitation seemed to be originating from multiple threat actors, and exposure is likely to remain uneven, with SMEs with more limited cyber postures facing greater challenges in identifying and fixing vulnerable instances.

This, said Moodys, could increase the likelihood of a “long tail” of individual cyber compromises affecting organisations for months to come.

According to threat intel company Cyfirma, there is also now evidence that PHP2Shell is attracting the interest of nation-state affiliated threat actors. The firm’s researchers said they were confident that a North Korean-nexus threat actor associated with the infamous Lazarus Group is “actively staging a global offensive campaign” against vulnerable, internet-facing PHP runtimes.

In addition to merely applying the patches, this means security teams should also be activating threat detection and response procedures to ascertain whether or not a breach is in progress.

title: UK secrecy over AI in immigration and asylum decisions under fire
raw_text:
The government is using AI in “near total secrecy” to police immigration and border crossings and is routinely invoking “national security” to refuse to answer questions on its use of automated technology, it is claimed.

MPs and campaigners warned today that secrecy around the Home Office’s use of AI in asylum and immigration meant there was little accountability over the UK’s use of the technology or its effectiveness.

Migrants and people crossing into the UK were at risk of discrimination, biased decision making and of being wrongly identified by facial-recognition systems, according to research by the Open Rights Group (ORG).

The campaign group warns in a 100-page report that the government is using “technical fixes” – what it calls “tech no-solutionism” – to implement policy decisions around “the complex human phenomenon of migration”.

A Home Office spokesperson said that artificial intelligence is just one of the tools available and does not replace or automate the role of human decision makers.

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” the spokesperson added.

“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

title: Employees must be empowered to refuse AI tools at work, says UTAW
raw_text:
Employees should be empowered to refuse the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools at work, says the tech worker union, after finding employers are using the technology to intensify workloads, eliminate junior hiring and rationalise redundancies.

Conducted by the United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) union – a branch of the Communication Workers Union (CWU) – the AI workers’ inquiry 2026 explores how AI tools are reshaping labour practices from the perspective of workers throughout the tech sector.

Focused less on the technology’s functionality and more on who controls and benefits from it, the inquiry found that AI technology was “a largely negative force” in the workplace, leading to a widespread deskilling and degrading of expertise, expanded surveillance, less accountability for managers and weaker job security.

The worker-led inquiry also found that AI, despite being touted as a productivity-boosting technology that can reduce working time, is being used in practice to increase and intensify people’s workloads.

All of this is taking place, it added, without workers having a meaningful say over how AI technologies are introduced.

“Workers stressed that positive uses depend on their ability to decide for themselves how to engage with AI,” said a report on the inquiry’s findings. “The central problem is not simply whether AI works well, but how it is introduced, controlled, measured and used by employers. Put simply, it is useful only when one gets to choose if and how to use them.”

It added that workers must be actively empowered to defend and extend their rights over how AI is used, which should include being given “enforceable power” over how it is deployed in the workplace, as an antidote to its unilateral imposition from management.

‘Testing ground’

UTAW highlighted how, according to inquiry participants, senior management teams do not understand the tools they are mandating, and are using staff as a “testing ground” for tools that often either slow down or worsen the work they claim to speed up or improve.

The unilateral imposition of AI, UTAW added, is also part of a wider trend where AI is being used to reduce headcounts and avoid hiring, while distributing the remaining work to fewer employees under tighter deadlines.

“At first glance, companies are carrying out redundancies (both mass layoffs and small regular redundancy exercises) and claiming this is because ‘AI is replacing the need for workers’,” it said.

“Workers on the inside report that layoffs are more often to maintain revenue in the face of rising inflation, to increase company valuation by manipulating financial indices, or even to cover the cost of GenAI [generative AI] platform subscriptions.

“These so-called AI efficiencies are an excuse to obfuscate a reality where skilled staff are replaced with new tools that do not work well while workers who survive redundancy pick up the ever-intensifying slack.”

For those at the start of their careers, UTAW also highlighted how AI is undermining their ability to develop skills, because they are either becoming too reliant on the tech themselves, or their employer is outsourcing their work – which would help them develop foundational skills – to automation.

“Junior workers and those without strong foundational skills are becoming overly reliant on tools such as agents and assistants,” it said. “There is no incentive or time for juniors to learn the necessary technical and critical thinking skills; work intensification means they are increasingly being denied a sounding board to chat through problems.

“Employers are using LLMs [large language models] as a substitute for training their employees, obscuring gaps in subject-matter expertise and skills … The long-term trajectory is a loss of expertise and skills across the sector.”

Policy proposals

As a result of its findings, UTAW has made a number of policy proposals for AI at work.

These include protecting employees from disciplinary and performance processes which are based on how much they are using (or not using) AI tools; strengthening redundancy protections so employers cannot use AI adoption as cover for offshoring or outsourcing; and introducing a statutory duty on employers to “meaningfully consult” workers before AI tools are deployed.

It added that, where collective bargaining agreements exist, employers must have a duty to negotiate on AI deployments and their associated effects.

Where these agreements do not exist, UTAW said that workers must still be given a right to refuse AI “where there are professional, ethical, environmental, equality, accessibility, safety, religious, mental health or quality concerns” around its use.

The codification of a right to refuse should also be accompanied by protections for workers that refuse, question or otherwise criticise an employer’s use of AI.

A number of other proposals also called for increased transparency around AI deployments at work.

This includes more consistent disclosures on its environmental impacts, such as “energy use, water use, datacentre dependency, infrastructure demand and supply-chain impacts”; the publication of various pre-deployment impact assessments; and prohibiting the use of opaque, AI-driven work evaluations.

To ensure employers are held accountable, UTAW concluded there is a need to establish a new regulatory authority on AI at work, which has statutory powers to investigate, enforce and sanction both employers and their technology providers.

“The authority should have the power to require employers to disclose AI systems, pause deployment, carry out impact assessments, consult workers and their unions, remedy harm, and withdraw deployed systems,” it said, adding that any governance board “should include expert worker and trade union representation equal to the number of representatives of employers, civil servants and academics”.

title: ‘Blackmail’ call as Warwickshire council approves £9m Microsoft renewal
raw_text:
Warwickshire County Council’s Reform-run cabinet has approved the procurement of a three-year Microsoft 365 licence renewal worth about £9m. The move was dubbed “blackmail” by its former leader as the approval went through.

The decision report – introduced by Reform councillor Michael Bannister – commits the council to a renewal agreement that runs from June 2027 to May 2030. The cost is roughly £3m a year, and that’s about £375,000, or 15%, more than the council pays currently. Bannister attributed the rise principally to Microsoft’s pricing changes across the public sector, after the previous renewal had deferred increases by continuing existing national pricing arrangements.

Warwickshire County Council – which rolled out Microsoft cloud in 2019 – buys through the government’s Microsoft aggregation route, which uses collective public sector buying power to secure pricing. Confirmation of the award is subject to a licence count review of active users, allocations and optional products. 

The report prepared for council cabinet approval describes the licences as “business critical”, in that they underpin “core productivity, collaboration, information management, security and analytics capabilities”, as well as cyber security, data protection and the groundwork for automation and artificial intelligence. Around 900 licences are to be charged to the relevant business areas, with further optional products potentially pushing the cost higher.

Green councillor Keith Kondakor, who represents Weddington, framed the decision as paying Microsoft for software the council would not own. Holding up a floppy disk he bought more than 40 years ago, he said: “When we bought Microsoft products in 1983, we owned them. You couldn’t get trapped, because once you bought your DOS, you got your DOS.”

His point was to draw a contrast with today’s subscription licensing. “The problem now is that we’re getting trapped into paying licence fees. We licence for a year or three years and then Microsoft can whack the price up,” he said.

He noted the French government is moving away from Microsoft, and warned: “If you are beholden to an American corporation, things can change.”

Rob Howard, Reform UK’s former council leader now serving as portfolio holder for economy, replied. He did not dispute the framing. “You’ve echoed what we were talking about in our pre-meeting,” he said. “I think we are all shocked about the amount of money this is going to cost us. We have no choice on this occasion, I’m afraid.”

His reasoning was that there was too little time to stand up an alternative before the May 2027 expiry. But he accepted the longer-term risk. “You’re right, we don’t want to be held with this sort of blackmail over the next 10 years. It is going to be more next time round,” he said.

The exchange came as the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) considers designating Microsoft’s business software ecosystem with strategic market status, while Microsoft contests the premise of the investigation.

The report warned that failing to approve the procurement risked “poorer commercial outcomes and disruption to essential digital services”. It also flagged that the agreement may overlap with local government reorganisation, with licence numbers, transfers and potential duplicate costs to be resolved before award.

The decision approves the procurement in principle. Any actual award rests with the executive director for resources, subject to affordability, completion of procurement and legal and financial assurance, while the extra £375,000 a year still has to be found within the budget.
